sec.title: Background
sec.p: Understanding genetic diversity and population structure is crucial for strategizing and enhancing breeding efficiency. Wheat, a globally cultivated crop, is a significant source of daily calories for humans. To overcome challenges such as extreme climatic fluctuations, stagnant yields, and diminishing genetic variation, it is essential to develop diverse germplasms with new alleles. Triticum sphaerococcum, an underutilized ancient hexaploid wheat species, shows promise for contributing beneficial alleles. However, the genetic diversity of its germplasms remains unstudied. This is the first report where we have examined the genetic diversity and population structure of 116 T. sphaerococcum accessions using a 35 K SNP Array. The objective of this study is to apply these findings to improve wheat breeding programs.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Analysis of the population’s genetic structure identified four potential subpopulations, which was supported by principal coordinate analysis. Allele neutrality tests showed an abundance of intermediate genotypes, suggesting that many beneficial alleles are maintained through balancing selection. Among the three subgenomes, subgenome B exhibited the highest genetic diversity. AMOVA (Analysis of Molecular Variance) revealed significant variation both among (35%) and within (65%) the four subpopulations. The high genetic differentiation between subpopulations was corroborated by a moderate level of haploid migrant numbers (Nm = 1.286), indicating sufficient gene flow. SP4 emerged as the most diverse subpopulation, showing the highest values for allelic pattern indices due to its larger size and higher percentage of polymorphic loci. The D subgenome displayed a faster linkage disequilibrium (LD) decay rate compared to the A and B subgenomes. Haplotype block analysis identified 260 haplotype blocks of varying sizes distributed across the genome.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: This research demonstrates that Indian dwarf wheat accessions, sourced from three distinct gene banks and local collections, possess considerable genetic diversity. These germplasm collections offer valuable opportunities to investigate their unexplored genetic potential. They can be utilized in wheat improvement initiatives to tackle both present and future breeding challenges. Furthermore, these accessions can introduce new alleles to broaden the genetic base of modern wheat varieties, enhancing their overall diversity.

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Wheat being one of the most widely grown and consumed crop across the world provides a fifth of global food calories and proteins [1]. The complex genome composition of bread wheat produces many hurdles in fully understanding the genetic complexity and dissecting agronomically and nutritionally important traits for their use in breeding programs. Genetic variability in the natural populations (landraces, crop wild relatives, etc.) holds great potential for their use in breeding for biotic and abiotic stress tolerance, increasing grain yield, and improving grain nutritional profile [2]. Plant breeding highly depends on the selection of elite lines which is possible only when diverse genotypes are available with the breeders. As genetic diversity diminishes across farmed cultivars, the susceptibility of crops to various stresses increases, particularly in the context of climate change and extreme climatic adversities. Therefore, it is essential to produce climate-resilient crop varieties particularly of wheat as it is the most important grain crop cultivated.

Wheat cultivars have increased yields and adapted to various climates, but at the cost of reduced genetic diversity [3]. This threatens the development of improved cultivars to feed the growing global population. The Rht genes introduced during the Green Revolution significantly increased kernel numbers in semi-dwarf genotypes [4]. The FAO World Information and Early Warning System reports 818,746 wheat accessions conserved in 162 Gene Banks across 81 countries [5]. These diverse collections offer ways to harness genetic variability to improve wheat breeding objectives. Crop wild relatives (CWR) and landraces have adapted to challenging environments, but their resilience mechanisms are poorly understood, limiting their use in breeding programs [6, 7]. Challenges include identifying valuable genetic traits and managing linkage drag when integrating them into elite germplasm [3]. Given reduced genetic diversity and increasing threats to wheat production, a ‘second green revolution’ utilizing inherent resources and genetic diversity understanding is crucial [8, 9].

Landraces are locally adapted domesticated species offering genetic resources for agricultural challenges [10]. Along with crop wild relatives, they provide extensive genetic variation for traits like yield potential, stability, and nutritional quality, especially under stress and climate change. Despite their potential to improve modern cultivars, landraces and crop wild relatives remain underutilized in modern breeding programs [11, 12]. Indian dwarf wheat (T. sphaerococcum Percival, 2n = 6x = 42) is an underutilized species. Archaeological evidence from carbonized grains found in Rohira village, Punjab, dating from approximately 2,000 to 1,700 B.C., suggests that T. sphaerococcum was under cultivation during the Harappan civilization in the north-western Indian subcontinent because of its tolerance to drought, salinity and low fertility conditions [13]. Native to northwestern India and southern Pakistan, it belongs to the same naked wheat group as common wheat. Josekutty [14] identified three potential origins of T. sphaerococcum: a mutational event in T. aestivum, hybridization between T. parvicoccum (sphaerococcum-type tetraploid wheat) and Aegilops species, or a cross between spherical-grained mutant T. turgidum and Ae. tauchii. Among these theories, the mutation in T. aestivum is the most probable explanation. Historically, this species was cultivated for its suitability to arid, warm regions and regional dietary inclinations. However, its distribution and cultivation was significantly affected following the Green Revolution’s implementation of high-yielding wheat varieties and the species’ vulnerability to rust [15]. Despite its decline in cultivation, the genetic diversity found in T. sphaerococcum remains a vital resource for enhancing the resilience and nutritional quality of modern wheat crops. This species is one of the ancestral forms in the evolutionary history of bread wheat making it a highly valuable reference population to investigate the recent adaptation of bread wheat [16]. The distinctive characteristics of this species, such as spherical grains, robust and short culms, and upright leaves [17], as well as resilience to abiotic stress [18], are attributable to the pleiotropic effects of a single locus, Sphaerococcum 1 (S1), located on chromosome 3D. To date, only a limited number of accessions of this species have been utilized for the evaluation of genetic variability concerning parameters such as grain and nutritional quality [19] and for variety development [20]. Thirty-four T. sphaerococcum accessions from the Indian National Genebank showed considerable variation in grain quality, encompassing protein, iron, and zinc content [19]. Among the 116 accessions of this species studied by Gaikwad et al. [15], there was a notable amount of variation in grain yield, yield contributing traits, and a few physiological traits such as canopy temperature and normalized difference vegetative index (NDVI). Incorporating these variations into elite materials will broaden the genetic base, creating novel allele combinations for breeding programs. There is a possibility that T. sphaerococcum varieties derived from the present-day accessions endemic to India and Pakistan will not be widely cultivated in modern agriculture and may even vanish in the future. Preserving the Indian dwarf wheat necessitates multiple years of methodical selective improvement. The procedure of targeted breeding with this species will involve gradual selection over several years, whereas reckless selection can take decades to complete. The natural variations in landraces underscore the need to understand their genetic architecture through molecular marker-based studies. It is also crucial to conserve more of these landraces in publicly accessible repositories with proper cataloguing, to facilitate their use in breeding programs aimed at addressing various objectives. Understanding the genetic diversity of Indian dwarf wheat is therefore crucial for identifying and conserving accessions with beneficial genotypic frameworks [21].

Compared to the conventional molecular markers, single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) offer more precise estimates of population-level diversity, greater power for identifying groups in clustering methods, and the ability to account for local adaptations as they provide a more accurate representation of genome-wide variations [22]. SNP arrays are high-throughput, cost-efficient, and automatically genotyping assay, making them suitable for various studies like association mapping, linkage-map construction, genetic diversity and population structure analyses, and gene mapping [23, 24] Furthermore, SNP array data is relatively easy to analyze compared to data generated using NGS-based technologies, particularly when considering labour-intensive NGS library preparation and downstream bioinformatics data analysis investment for accurate SNP calling [24]. In the present study, we used a collection of 116 T. sphaerococcum accessions collected from three gene banks across the world to study the genetic diversity and population structure along with genetic differentiation among and within subpopulations using the Affymetrix 35 K Axiom Wheat Breeders’ Array. We, at the ICAR-India Agricultural Research Institute in New Delhi, have the most accessions of this species in one location than any other institution worldwide.

sec.title: Plant material
sec.p: A set of 116 accessions of T. sphaerococcum were sourced from three gene banks and used in the present study. Details of these accessions are available in Additional file 1: Table S1. Specifically, 32 accessions were obtained from IPK Germany, 27 from the Institute of Plant Genetic Resources “Konstantin Malkov” in Sadovo, Bulgaria, 31 from the National Small Grain Collections, USDA, 22 from Punjab Agricultural University in Ludhiana, India, and 5 accessions were collected from the farmers’ fields.

sec.title: DNA extraction and genotyping
sec.p: Genomic DNA was extracted from young leaves following the CTAB protocol [25], and DNA concentration and purity were assessed with a NanoDrop Spectrophotometer. The DNA samples were genotyped using the 35 K Axiom® Wheat Breeders’ Array following the manufacturer’s guidelines. The SNP array included 35,143 SNP markers, which were filtered to remove unmapped markers in Excel. Beagle v5.4 [26] with default settings was used to impute the missing marker information. The imputed marker data was used to filter markers with a minor allele frequency (MAF) of less than 5%, and markers with over 30% heterozygosity in TASSEL v5.9.24 [27]. This filtering process resulted in a subset of highly informative 11,680 SNP markers used for downstream analyses.

sec.title: Genetic analysis of SNP markers
sec.p: Genetic diversity analysis was performed using the filtered SNP subset in TASSEL v5.9.24 to derive nucleotide diversity (π) per base pair and Tajima’s D statistic with a window size of 50 markers and step size of 10 markers. These parameters provide insights into the genetic structure, neutrality, and evolutionary history of the population under study [28]. Gene diversity (GD), polymorphism information content (PIC), and MAF were calculated using POWERMARKER v3.25 [29].

sec.title: Population structure
sec.p: The population structure of the T. sphaerococcum accessions was inferred using the Bayesian method implemented in STRUCTURE v2.3.4 [30]. Ten independent runs were performed for each K value (ranging from 1 to 10), with a burn-in period of 100,000 iterations followed by 100,000 Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) replications. The stand-alone version of STRUCTURE HARVESTER [31] was used to determine the most likely number of subpopulations (K), utilizing an ad-hoc statistic, ΔK, based on the rate of change in the log probability of the data between successive K values [32]. The genetic distance between the accessions was estimated in TASSEL v5.9.24 which was used to visualize the neighbour-joining phylogenetic tree based on the inferred number of K from STRUCTURE HARVESTER using the web interface of iTOL v5 [33]. In addition, a panel of 223 bread wheat advanced breeding lines were used to create a neighbour-joining tree to display the phylogenetic differentiation of the T. sphaerococcum accessions from the T. aestivum accessions as both the species belong to the same hexaploid wheat group.

sec.title: Analysis of molecular variance (AMOVA) and genetic diversity indices
sec.p: For this analysis, we included SNPs based on their PIC values. Only SNPs with PIC ≥ 0.15 were selected, ensuring that the markers used provided reliable genetic diversity information for the population structure analysis. The number of subpopulations inferred from STRUCTURE analysis was considered for AMOVA. The genetic indices such as different alleles (Na), number of effective alleles (Ne), Shannon’s index (I), observed heterozygosity (ho), diversity index (h), unbiased diversity index (uh), and percentage of polymorphic loci (PPL) were calculated. The AMOVA and estimation of genetic indices were performed using GenAlEx v6.51 [34]. Principal Coordinate Analysis (PCoA) was conducted using Nei’s genetic distance [35].

sec.title: Linkage disequilibrium and haplotype block analysis
sec.p: Linkage disequilibrium (LD) between each pair of 11,680 SNPs with a sliding window of 50 markers was estimated as the squared allele frequency correlation (r2) in TASSEL v5.9.24 and LD decay for each subgenome and whole genome was visualized in R Studio. To visualize the relationship between linkage disequilibrium (LD) decay and physical distance, a locally weighted linear regression (LOESS) curve was generated using the ‘loess’ function in R. The LD decay rate was defined as the physical distance at which the r² value decreased to 50% of its mean maximum value [36]. For haplotype block analysis, the number and size of haplotype blocks in each chromosome were estimated in Haploview 4.2 software [37] using the default settings. The haplotype blocks were defined using a confidence interval method as proposed by Gabriel et al. [38].

sec.title: Distribution of SNP markers across the T. sphaerococcum accessions
sec.p: The T. sphaerococcum accessions were tested with a total of 35,143 SNPs from the 35 K Axiom Wheat Breeders’ Array. After quality filtering, 11,680 high-quality informative SNPs were retained, which were well distributed across the genome (Fig. 1). The SNP distribution was analyzed in a window size interval of 1 Mb across the chromosomes. Subgenome B had the highest SNP count, comprising approximately 40% (4,612 SNPs), while subgenome D had the lowest, with about 28% (3,323 SNPs). Subgenome A contained 3,745 SNPs, making up around 32%. The number of SNPs per chromosome varied from 210 on chromosome 4D to 855 on chromosome 2B (Table 1).

sec.title: Assessment of genetic variation and evolutionary metrics
sec.p: In this study, gene diversity (GD) ranged from 0.098 to 0.5, with chromosome 1B showing the highest mean GD (0.234) and chromosome 4D the lowest (0.187). Subgenome B exhibited the highest mean GD (0.224) across the whole genome. Polymorphism information content (PIC) values fell between 0.093 and 0.375, with chromosome 1B having the highest mean PIC (0.199) and chromosome 4D the lowest (0.165), as illustrated in Fig. 2.

caption.p: Gene diversity and polymorphism information content of the T. sphaerococcum accessions. The chromosome-wise SNP count of the three different subgenomes is represented as bars in three different colors on the primary axis. GD and PIC values are depicted by red and yellow line graphs on the secondary axis, respectively

sec.p: The genome-wide averages for GD and PIC were 0.216 and 0.187, respectively. The observed nucleotide diversity (π/bp) ranged from 0.144 to 0.366, with chromosome 1B having the highest mean value of 0.236, and chromosome 2D the lowest at 0.195. Nucleotide diversity levels were similar across all three subgenomes (Table 1). According to Kimura’s neutral theory of molecular evolution [39], most evolutionary changes result from the fixation of neutral mutations through genetic drift rather than natural selection. Tajima’s D test compares nucleotide diversity (π/bp) and the number of segregating sites (θ); under neutrality, these measures should be approximately equal. Deviations suggest either balancing selection (positive values) or purifying selection (negative values). The population mutation rate, or expected nucleotide diversity, was 0.187 genome-wide. Tajima’s D values ranged from − 0.729 to 2.967, with chromosome 2D showing the lowest mean value (0.121) and chromosome 1B the highest (0.814). Among the subgenomes, subgenome B had the highest Tajima’s D (0.619), followed by subgenome A (0.429), and subgenome D had the lowest (0.405). The mean π/bp and Tajima’s D across the entire genome were 0.218 and 0.504, respectively (Table 1).

sec.title: Population structure and principal coordinate analysis
sec.p: To analyze the population structure of the 116 T. sphaerococcum accessions, delta K (ΔK) values were used to determine the most likely number of subpopulations (K). Various cluster numbers (K, ranging from 1 to 10) were plotted against their ΔK values, with K = 4 showing the highest ΔK (720.878) (Fig. 3). The inferred number of clusters was then used to visualize the genetic membership of each cluster among the 116 accessions by grouping the genotypes based on the Q-matrix.

caption.p: Population structure of the 116 T. sphaerococcum accessions: a Evanno’s method was used to determine the most likely number of clusters in the population, identifying K = 4 based on the highest ad-hoc statistic, ΔK, at K = 4. b A bar plot representing the four subpopulations based on the Q-matrix, where columns on the x-axis represent individuals of the population

sec.p: Using the inferred clusters from the STRUCTURE HARVESTER output and the genetic distances calculated in TASSEL, a neighbour-joining phylogenetic tree was constructed to visualize the clusters (Fig. 4). The four subpopulations were labelled SP1, SP2, SP3, and SP4, comprising 19, 14, 35, and 48 accessions, respectively. Principal Coordinate Analysis (PCoA) based on the first two principal coordinates (PCo1 at 26.76% and PCo2 at 13.67%) separated the 116 accessions into four clusters (subpopulations) (Fig. 4).

caption.p: Clustering of the 116 T. sphaerococcum accessions into four subpopulations: a Principal Coordinate Analysis (PCoA) separated the subpopulations, indicated by different colors, by plotting the eigenvalues of PCo1 (26.76%) against PCo2 (13.67%). b Neighbor-Joining (NJ) phylogenetic tree constructed based on the genetic distance among individuals, visualized with different colors (Blue: SP1, Red: SP2, Green: SP3, Purple: SP4). Based on the PCoA and NJ tree construction, SP4 was observed to be the most diverse and exhibited the highest amount of subpopulation variation

sec.p: The phylogenetic analysis conducted using an unrooted NJ-tree effectively differentiated the 116 T. sphaerococcum accessions from the 223 T. aestivum accessions (Fig. 5). The resulting NJ-tree exhibited two distinct clades, clearly demarcating the phylogenetic divergence between the two hexaploid wheat species.

caption.p: Phylogenetic analysis of T. sphaerococcum and T. aestivum accessions. The clade with branches and individuals labeled in red includes the accessions from T. sphaerococcum while those labeled in green comprises of T. aestivum. This partition underscores the genetic differentiation and evolutionary relationship between the two hexaploid wheat species

sec.title: Population genetic differentiation and allelic patterns
sec.p: The four subpopulations identified from the STRUCTURE analysis were used to calculate AMOVA and genetic diversity indices using GenAlEx macros in Excel. For robust results, 6,958 markers with PIC values of ≥ 0.15 were selected. AMOVA results revealed significant variation within and among the subpopulations. Total variation was divided into 35% among subpopulations and 65% within subpopulations (Table 2). The overall genetic differentiation coefficient (Fst) among the populations was 0.349 that explained the variation among the subpopulations. The haploid number of migrants (Nm) was 1.286 ± 0.045, indicating moderate gene exchange between subpopulations, with values above 1 suggesting sufficient gene flow to counteract genetic drift. In addition, the Fst estimates for each cluster was obtained from individual runs of STRUCTURE software for K = 4, and the mean Fst value for each subpopulation is presented in Table 3. The value of Fst ranges from 0 to 1, with 0 indicating no differentiation between the subpopulations while 1 indicates complete differentiation. SP1 exhibited the highest Fst value (0.7944) indicating less variation among the genotypes within this subpopulation while SP4 had the lowest Fst value (0.4564) which indicates.

sec.p: The average number of different alleles (Na) and effective alleles (Ne) across the population were 1.454 and 1.246, respectively. Shannon’s index (I), observed heterozygosity (Ho), diversity index (He), and unbiased diversity index (uHe) across all loci and subpopulations were 0.222, 0.103, 0.147, 0.149, and 0.262, respectively. SP4 exhibited the highest diversity based on these indices, while SP1 showed the least diversity, likely due to its smaller number of individuals (Table 4). The total percentage of polymorphic loci (PPL) was 45.31%, with SP4 having the highest proportion (99.99%) and SP1 the lowest (8.48%).

sec.title: Estimation of linkage disequilibrium and haplotype patterns
sec.p: For estimating linkage disequilibrium (LD), the total set of filtered SNPs (11,680 markers) was used to calculate the pairwise squared frequency correlations (r²) in TASSEL for every marker pair within a sliding window of 50 markers. The r² values were plotted against physical distances to visualize LD decay patterns, defined as the physical distance at which the r² value decreased to 50% of its mean maximum value. The rate of LD decay was fastest in subgenome D (7.11 Mb), followed by subgenome A (7.59 Mb) and subgenome B (7.91 Mb). The overall genome LD decay occurred at 7.62 Mb (Fig. 6). For haplotype analysis, the confidence interval method was used to define haplotype blocks. Chromosome 4D had the lowest number of haplotype blocks (1), while chromosome 2D had the highest (32) (Fig. 7). Most haplotype blocks were defined by only 2 SNPs, and the size of the blocks increased with the number of SNPs in LD forming the blocks (Additional file 2: Table S2).

caption.p: Estimation of Linkage Disequilibrium (LD) decay rate for the a A subgenome, b B subgenome, c D subgenome, and d whole genome. The LD decay rate was observed to be the fastest for the D subgenome in the panel of 116 T. sphaerococcum accessions, based on 11,680 markers

Haplotype block analysis across the genome revealed the highest number of haplotype blocks on chromosome 2D. The average number of SNPs per block, illustrated by a red line graph on the secondary axis, showed that most blocks were defined by only 2 SNPs. The size of the blocks (kb) was determined by the number of SNPs defining them and the physical distance between the SNPs

sec.title: Genetic diversity of the Indian dwarf wheat accessions
sec.p: Indian dwarf wheat is an underutilized hexaploid species well-adapted to Indian conditions and valued by farmers for its quality traits in preparing traditional food products. However, the domestication and the Green Revolution have largely replaced it with modern cultivars across the country. Despite this, Indian dwarf wheat holds a vast array of unexplored variations for many beneficial traits [12, 15, 18], which could be crucial in surpassing the genetic limitations of these traits. Genetic diversity analysis is essential to fully exploit these variations. In this study, we utilized the 35 K Axiom Wheat Breeders’ Array to genotype T. sphaerococcum accessions, chosen for its high density and comprehensive genome coverage. Exploiting these accessions could aid in identifying diverse sources of novel alleles for wheat improvement programs. We used a total of 11,680 informative SNPs, finding the lowest frequency in the D subgenome and the highest in the B subgenome, consistent with previous studies [40]. The SNPs were more densely distributed in non-centromeric regions, where the recombination rate is lower. The older subgenomes, B and A, exhibited a higher number of SNPs, likely due to earlier gene flow and gene duplications, which have led to the accumulation of more mutations over time [41, 42].

The analysis of gene diversity (GD) and Polymorphism Information Content (PIC) reveals crucial insights into the genetic variability and marker informativeness. All three subgenomes exhibited similar trends for both GD and PIC, with subgenome B having the highest mean values, followed by A and D. The higher mean GD in the B subgenome compared to A and D indicates that it contains greater genetic variation, aligning with previous findings [43, 44]. Although all three subgenomes had positive mean values for Tajima’s D, indicating balancing selection, the higher values for subgenome B, followed by A and D, suggest that subgenome B is more genetically diverse and contains numerous favorable alleles [45, 46].

sec.title: Population structure and genetic differentiation
sec.p: Classifying the accessions based on molecular markers such as SNPs offers significant advantages over phenotype-based clustering, as phenotypes are influenced by genotype, environment, and their interactions, while SNP-based clustering groups accessions solely on genetic differences. Analyzing population structure significantly enhances the understanding of genetic diversity and improves the accuracy of association mapping by using population structure information as a covariate to minimize the discovery of false associations [21, 47]. In our study, we identified four subpopulations, which can be attributed to historical recombination events, genetic bottlenecks, and natural and artificial selection pressures [48, 49]. Principal Coordinates Analysis (PCoA) utilized a dissimilarity matrix to compute eigenvalues, classifying the accessions into four subpopulations by plotting the eigenvalues of PCo1 against PCo2. The PCoA results were consistent with those of the Neighbor-Joining (NJ) tree. The phylogenetic analysis of the T. sphaerococcum and T. aestivum accessions displayed a clear distinction between the two species. This result is in accordance with the findings of Zhou et al. [16], where they had conducted a phylogenetic analysis to observe the evolutionary relationship between 25 Triticum subspecies and reported that Indian dwarf wheat was basal to 96% of bread wheat in the phylogeny of D lineage.

Our study utilized a filtered set of 11,680 SNPs to avoid overestimating the number of subpopulations while maintaining sufficient power to distinguish individuals based on genetic differences. PIC, which measures marker informativeness, was used to further filter the SNPs (≥ 0.15), resulting in a subset of markers capable of effectively assessing genetic diversity among subpopulations. AMOVA results indicated significantly high levels of genetic diversity within subpopulations and moderate levels among them. The genetic diversity within subpopulations is attributed to the selection for agronomically important traits by farmers and breeders mainly influenced by local adaptation and environmental pressures [50], while diversity among subpopulations is primarily due to gene flow [51]. The Nm value of 1.286 for the panel indicates a moderate level of genetic variation among subpopulations attributed to genetic exchange, suggesting that these accessions have been utilized in breeding programs to a small extent [23]. Genetic differentiation in T. sphaerococcum is associated with specific adaptive genes such as VRN-D4, which shows evidence of positive selection [52]. This genetic adaptation is crucial for the species’ survival in specific ecological niches, especially given current climate change and agricultural challenges. According to Frakham et al. [53], Fst values exceeding 0.15 indicate significant genetic differentiation due to population structure. Significant divergence was observed within each T. sphaerococcum subpopulation. However, the moderate Fst value (0.349) observed among the four subpopulations suggests moderate genetic differentiation between subpopulations. This explains the higher variation within the subpopulations as compared to variation among the subpopulations observed in the present study. SP4 exhibited the highest values for all assessed allelic pattern indices, reflecting a greater degree of variation within this subpopulation due to its larger size. For instance, Shannon’s information index (I) is an effective measure of diversity, reflecting not only allele richness but also their distribution within the population. The unbiased expected heterozygosity (uHe), which accounts for sample size, provides a more accurate depiction of the genetic diversity in SP4. Additionally, the percentage of polymorphic loci (PPL) is a crucial population genetics metric that highlights the genetic variability in SP4, indicating that this group may be less susceptible to genetic drift and inbreeding depression compared to populations with lower diversity. Overall, the comprehensive analysis of genetic diversity indices emphasizes the potential benefits of using these materials, particularly accessions from SP4, in breeding programs aimed at developing new and improved wheat cultivars with desirable traits through breeding and conservation programs.

sec.title: Linkage disequilibrium and haplotypes in the panel
sec.p: Assessing the extent of linkage disequilibrium (LD) and its decay rate in any panel is crucial, as it influences the selection of markers and the resolution of association mapping [54]. We measured the magnitude of LD in each of the three subgenomes individually and across the entire genome to gain insights into the genetic architecture and recombination history. Previous studies have indicated that LD decay occurs more rapidly in subgenome B compared to the other two subgenomes [55, 56]. However, our findings revealed a faster LD decay rate in subgenome D, followed by subgenomes A and B, which aligns with results from earlier research [57, 58]. The D subgenome typically shows faster LD decay due to its higher and more uniform recombination distribution along chromosomes [59]. However, in the current T. sphaerococcum population, all three subgenomes show similar LD decay patterns, likely due to this species’ limited use in modern breeding programs. The discrepancies in LD decay patterns among the subgenomes can be attributed to variations in the study materials, levels of gene flow, population stratifications, and the degree of selection pressure.

Identifying haplotype blocks in wheat is essential for genomic research, as it helps elucidate genetic diversity and enhances breeding strategies. Haplotype blocks are contiguous genome segments inherited together due to linkage disequilibrium (LD). In our study, we identified 260 haplotype blocks using a stringent confidence interval method [38]. Other, less stringent methods, such as the spine method and the four-gamete rule, can identify a greater number of blocks, which is beneficial for haplotype-based association mapping. Identifying these blocks can significantly improve the precision of genomic selection and deepen the understanding of trait associations in wheat. Haplotype blocks have been effectively used to understand genetic diversity in Central European winter wheat landraces, highlighting the crucial role of haplotype variation in preserving genetic resources for future breeding strategies [60]. Mourad et al. [61] showed that blocks enriched with significant SNPs can reduce redundancy and enhance the power of association studies, improving the identification of genetic markers linked to stem rust resistance. GWAS combined with transcriptomic analysis revealed genetic loci that influence seminal root growth, identifying key genes associated with the trait through haplotype analysis, demonstrating the complex role of haplotypes in trait expression [62]. Thus, the findings of this study offer comprehensive insights into the genetic diversity of these accessions and present opportunities for their application in wheat breeding programs to tackle current and future breeding challenges.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: The genetic diversity analysis of Indian dwarf wheat (T. sphaerococcum) accessions using the 35 K Axiom Wheat Breeders’ Array has revealed significant variability across the subgenomes. The B subgenome demonstrated the highest gene diversity (GD) and Polymorphism Information Content (PIC), indicating its rich genetic variation and potential as a source of novel alleles for wheat improvement programs. The population structure analysis identified four distinct subpopulations, reflecting historical recombination events and selection pressures. Notably, genotypes in SP4 exhibited the highest genetic diversity, making them ideal candidates for developing trait-based biparental mapping populations. The study’s findings on linkage disequilibrium (LD) and haplotype blocks provide critical insights for genomic selection and association mapping. The identification of 260 haplotype blocks underscores their importance in enhancing the precision of trait associations and improving breeding strategies. These results highlight the untapped genetic potential of T. sphaerococcum accessions, offering valuable resources for future wheat breeding programs aimed at overcoming current and future agricultural challenges employing genomic approaches such as genomic selection, GWAS, and marker-assisted selection.
